question: How should an adult survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a relative cope with the trauma?
asked: A sister wrote that she was sexually abused as a child by a family member, and now that she is an adult she is having several issues. She is asking for general advice and an Islamic understanding of what is going on.
answer:
Now, dear brothers and sisters, to be honest, this was a very, very difficult email to read. It was a very difficult question to stomach. I found it very difficult to read, I found it even more difficult to prepare, and I cannot even begin to fathom how difficult the situation would be for this sister and for all brothers and sisters who are in a similar situation.

So today is going to be a relatively lengthy response, because sadly, even though this is a specific email, I have been receiving such emails and hearing such matters literally since the time I began preaching and teaching, more than 20 years ago. Every few weeks or months another question comes up where somebody is asking a very sensitive question of this nature.

And really, we need to be more frank in our conversations. We need to educate our brothers and sisters, and especially give them some of the tools that they need to cope with what has happened to some of them. And we also need to break the taboo surrounding these topics, because us not talking about them compounds the problem. When we pretend that this doesn't exist in our community, this is just blatantly wrong. Wallahi, every single scholar out there, without exception, who is involved in the community will tell you personal anecdotes that have come up to them, horror stories of maybe even their own congregation members that have come up to them. This is something we are well aware of.

So why don't we talk about this publicly? Why don't we start educating both sides? I mean, maybe there's somebody out there, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah, who's thinking about such a matter. He needs to hear a khutbah. He needs to hear something; that is better than nothing. I mean, there's no guarantee it will stop him, but it definitely needs to be brought up. The fear of God needs to be placed in these people before they undertake this path.

On the flip side, you have a lot of people who have undergone such traumatic events, and they don't know what to do. They don't understand where to go. They themselves are having issues internally. And so to hear a lecture, even if it's going to be generic (today's lecture is all generic; the sister's case, I have made it such that we can extrapolate to other people as well), at least some lecture and some words of affirmation of their trauma and some practical steps is better than nothing.

So I'm hoping to start breaking this taboo. I'm hoping to at least begin this conversation, with the clear caveat, dear brothers and sisters, that obviously this is not my training. This is not my area of expertise. I will not be giving specific counseling or psychiatric help. That's not who I am or what I'm supposed to do. However, I can give generic Islamic advice, and inshallah generic advice, with the continual encouragement to go seek professional help.

I'm speaking today not just as a person who has studied a little bit of Islamic studies, but also as a parent to a parent, and as somebody who has just read too much and heard too much, a'udhu billah. Today's lecture honestly was very difficult for me to even prepare. It just brings up a lot of emotions in me, and I cannot even begin to fathom how others are coping with this. So bismillah, we begin in the name of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

So I want to begin by talking a little bit about your past. Dear sister, your email, I could sense from it a lot of pain, a lot of trauma, and I can only give you generic advice. I strongly, strongly advise you to seek the help of a professional trained counselor. I wish I could say it is wajib. I wish I could say that you must go. It's as close to "must" as possible. You are clearly in pain. You have undergone something that I can't even have words for. I could hardly read it, so how about yourself?

So there are people, dear sister, that are trained in dealing with this type of trauma. There has been a lot of research done, and there are people that have many hours of training in how to make you stronger and better, and how to help you overcome. And that discipline, that science, is not related necessarily to the religion of Islam. What I mean by this is that if you find a Muslim who's trained, alhamdulillah, great, but it's not necessary to go to a Muslim counselor. As long as you go to somebody who's going to give you good and generic advice, and in this particular area that you're going to, inshallah, anybody you go to is fine.

So we would appreciate if you could find a faith-based counselor, somebody who's trained in the area of sexual abuse and sexual trauma of youngsters. If you find somebody that is trained in counseling and is of a Muslim background, alhamdulillah. But to be honest, it's very rare to find one of our own specialized in counseling in this area.

And so what I'm asking of you, what I'm telling you, is: **do not feel ashamed at all to go seek help.** Dear sister, if my house was burgled (may Allah 'azza wa jall protect all of us in our houses), I would seek help from the police. All of us would. Something more precious than a house, something even more sanctified than the house, was transgressed, and that is your honor. Something far more precious than physical possessions was transgressed, and that is your sanctity. So why is there a sense in some people, a sense that society makes us feel, that there's something wrong if I have to get psychiatric help? And I'm telling you, there's nothing wrong.

Dear sister, your body was violated. Why would it be problematic to get help from somebody whom you can express to, who can help you cope with what has happened to you so many years ago? Do not feel ashamed of asking for help. I swear to you, I wish I could say it's wajib, but I can't. It's as close to wajib as I can say: you should get help. I can't help you in that regard; it's not my area of expertise. So please get some professional help. And from what I understand, most countries in the world, especially Western countries, have free helplines in this regard. So Google in your country; find out where you can get that type of help.

Also, dear sister, realize that what happened to you is not your fault. From your email, I can sense that you are an incredibly brave and strong woman. You shall survive. You survived the past, you shall survive through today, and you shall survive, inshallah, till the future, until Allah wills that we all have to leave on to the next life. But please do not have evil thoughts about finishing this life. That's not the way Muslims go down. We put our trust in Allah, and we have full trust that tomorrow is a better day than yesterday. We have our full trust that, inshallah ta'ala, our future is going to be brighter: that what's going to come to you is better than what happened in the past. You shall survive through this, and you shall be a stronger person and a better person and a more courageous person because of all that has happened.

And I want to say very explicitly, because you reference in your email that there's a sense of guilt coming from you, I want to say this as clearly as possible: **this is not your fault. This is not your fault.** You have nothing to do with the crime that occurred. You were the subject of that crime. The crime happened against you. You were not the one who perpetrated it; it was perpetrated against you. And psychiatrists say that self-blame is a very common symptom of abuse. You were a child. It's not your responsibility. Do not double guess and say, "I didn't do this, maybe I didn't do that enough." No, no, no, stop. Do not go down that route. You were a child. It's not your responsibility to do anything. It was his responsibility to not do something.

So you cannot and you should not go down this road of self-blaming or self-analysis, or thinking, "What if I had done this, then that?" Do not go down this. And you know what? In fact, our Prophet ﷺ even said to us adults: do not open the door of "what if." Do not say, "If only I had done this, then that would have happened," because that's just opening up the door to Shaytan. He said this to us as adults, that you're not supposed to do that. How much more so when you were a child?

And then maybe Shaytan comes to you, and this is all Shaytan making you even feel... You don't have to feel guilty. It's not your responsibility, what happened, what you did or what you did not do. You were a little boy or a little girl. It's not your prerogative. It's not your responsibility. So do not open this door of Shaytan, that you start feeling a sense of "maybe I did something wrong, maybe I didn't do enough." No, you were not an adult.

Now, we're not talking about somebody who's consensual, 30, 40, 50 years old. That's a totally different thing. Two consensual adults, definitely, I'm not going to be sugarcoating it; I'll say, you know what, both of you should have done this and that. But subhanAllah, as a child, no. We shut that door completely. You have zero guilt on you, nothing of this nature.

Also, the issue of depression and of thoughts, I mean, subhanAllah, I should be blunt here, thoughts of suicide and whatnot: not really. Again, dear sister, Allah says in the Qur'an, "Don't kill yourselves. Allah is ever merciful." In the very verse about suicide, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions His name, Rahman and Rahim. In the very verse that prohibits suicide, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala says, I am the Forgiving, I'm the Merciful, I'm the one who has rahmah. And rahmah is a compassion that is meant to bring benefit to you. So turn to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala and get help.

I keep on saying, and I'm going to say this so many times, this is not an area that most shaykhs and scholars and religious teachers... We were not taught this in the University of Medina or in Azhar or wherever you go. Islamic studies is a discipline that is meant to give you fatwas. It's meant to teach you theology. It's meant to derive tafsir and laws. It is not meant for counseling and therapy. And I've been saying this for the longest time: the majority of scholars are not trained to be therapists and counselors.

So do not go to a shaykh thinking that the shaykh is going to counsel you, unless the shaykh has training outside. I mean, obviously you can have multiple areas of expertise. That's why, please, the shaykh is not meant for the counseling. The shaykh is meant for Islamic advice, and generic. And even I am telling you: go to a counselor, go to somebody who is an actual professional.

Also, I always say that there are three Fs that really help: faith, family, and friends. Along with counseling, three Fs are always very helpful, and especially in that order: faith, family, and friends.

Faith: there is no doubt that faith is helpful. This does not mean that faith is going to be the end-all cure for every problem that you are facing. No, there are times you need medical help. There are times you need a therapist. Faith can only take you so far. But I'll tell you one thing: faith is never going to harm you. The more faith you have, it's never going to be to your detriment. True, you can have the highest faith in the world and you still have issues that have to be dealt with. So those are two separate things.

Nonetheless, generically, increase your connection with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. That's never going to harm you. Increase your du'as to Allah. Open your heart to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Have conversations with Him, especially in the middle of the night when everybody is asleep: you wake up and you have that prayer and that tahajjud with Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Also of the things that you can be doing is just extra dhikr and Qur'an and spirituality. So that's faith.

Family: find the family. We're going to come to this issue in part two of your question as well, but you must have some cousins or some people that you can get some love and comfort and validation from. And then close friends. So faith, family and friends, along with, of course, professional help.

Now, your email did not mention this, but I'm going to mention some other symptoms for others to benefit from. Studies show that such type of trauma that occurs, especially to a young child, leads to many problems. I already mentioned some of them, which is, for example, guilt and self-blame, and depression and suicidal thoughts. There are other problems also that are associated with this. Of them is eating disorders or substance abuse. So it's as if refuge is sought by overeating or by substance abuse, and of course that's not the way to go. It's not going to help in the long run.

Also, a lot of times it's common that there are trust issues; it's difficult to have trust with somebody. And again, that's fully understandable, because a child is supposed to trust every adult. When an adult, and especially a family member, breaks that trust, what do you think is going to happen to the psyche of that child? So again, this is understandable, and that's why we need trained counselors. We have lots of research done now. So much has been done of psychoanalysis, of psychiatric training, of hundreds of thousands of hours of on-the-field experiences that have been culled together, and there's a lot done. And frankly, again, truth be told, more has been done on this side of the Atlantic than on the other side. So take benefit from these types of counselors and therapists to help you develop in these trust issues.

It's also very common that relationships become problematic. So perhaps a young man or a young lady has suffered this trauma, and then they move on, they get married, but then they cannot form the connection with their spouse that they should. And again, this goes back to that trust issue. And then of course, obviously, a lot of times there are intimacy problems within marriage that perhaps even she or he is not even aware go back to that issue of childhood that they're struggling with. They think they've overcome it, they think they're fine, but then at that moment of intimacy, psychologically, subconsciously, a flashback happens. Something happens beyond their control. And of course the other partner might be totally unaware, might not even know what happened, and then that's going to cause problems in the marriage, because again, from his or her perspective: "What am I doing wrong? Why is this happening?" Etc., etc.

So that is why I keep on saying, dear sister (and of course I'm speaking to you, but through you I'm speaking to anybody who is in this situation): do not hesitate to get help from those that have spent lifetimes, trained for many, many hours. That's what their expertise is in. I can only give you generic advice. Go to them for specific advice. Be aware that not only is there nothing wrong with it, but on the contrary, I have had many cases of people that have come to me that have improved drastically, improved greatly after going through therapy from trained counselors. And so I speak firsthand, meaning through the people that I know, I speak firsthand that it can potentially be very, very effective.
